title: The Dal Khalsa, 1748
hookLine: at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar the bands united into one army under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia

lines: BANDS RIDE IN FROM EVERY SIDE.
cards: Horsemen are riding into Amritsar from every direction. Each group has its own leader, its own banner, its own story of the hard years; some leaders have quarreled.

Each band has survived by being quick and independent, answering to no one but its chief. Now they are all dismounting near the Harmandir, for a gathering Sikhs call the Sarbat Khalsa: the whole Khalsa, together.
On the table is a question that asks a lot of proud people. Should each of us keep riding alone? Today's word is their answer: Dal Khalsa.

teach.b: Dal means an army, a host. Dal Khalsa: the army of the Khalsa. This path met the name once before, beside the gurmata, the decision the gathering makes together.
Today, look at what it cost. Tradition says it was Nawab Kapur Singh, the humble leader who had once been fanning the sangat, who pressed for it. The scattered bands would become one army.

teach.h: EACH CHIEF STEPPED BACK A LITTLE.
teach.b: They wouldn't disappear: each chief kept his own band and his own riders. But they would answer to one command, and gather again at Amritsar to decide things together.
As head of that army, the gathering chose Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. So every chief gave something up. Not his men, not his name, but the right to do whatever he liked.

teach.h: UNITY IS EASY TO PRAISE, HARD TO DO.
teach.b: That's the hard part of unity: not agreeing it would help, but being the one who steps back so it can happen. Where did the Sikhs get the nerve to try? From something older than the army.
Guru Gobind Singh had founded the Khalsa as one body, with one initiation, drinking from one bowl.
And the Sikh scripture speaks again and again of the sangat, the company of the faithful, as the place where the Guru is found. The Dal Khalsa gave that idea saddles.
And the gathering decided in front of the Harmandir, with the Granth present.
Sikhs understand those decisions as made in the Guru's presence, not just a vote of the strongest.
When the bands rode out of Amritsar, they rode out as one army.

how: Sikhs still speak of the Sarbat Khalsa, a gathering of the whole community at Amritsar, as the place where the Panth decides together in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: the council of elders that wrote the Khalsa's rules down
the army of the Khalsa: the bands joined under one command
a single band of riders led by Nawab Kapur Singh

s: when the Dal Khalsa formed, the separate bands were broken up
each chief kept his own band, but they answered to one command.
the decision was made at Amritsar, near the Harmandir
Sikhs understand it as decided in the Guru's presence.
the gathering chose Jassa Singh Ahluwalia to head the Dal Khalsa
the gathering made him head of the one army.

games.q: you're a chief of your own Sikh band. your riders have survived the hard years by being fast and answering to no one. at the Sarbat Khalsa, they propose one army. what do you do?
o: keep riding alone: independence kept you alive.
join, keep your band, and answer to one command.
join only if you're made the commander.
games.why: tradition says the bands joined as one army under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. each chief kept his men but gave up doing whatever he liked.

practice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a team, a congregation, and notice where you've been riding alone in it.
Ask honestly what you'd give up, a little, for it to move together: an opinion held too tight, the need to be in charge. Just see it and breathe, and if you pray, say Waheguru with the group in mind.

wordCard.voice: Dal Khalsa. The army of the Khalsa: tradition says the scattered Sikh bands joined it at a Sarbat Khalsa in Amritsar, under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Dal Khalsa, the army of the Khalsa; dal means an army or host.

carryVoice: Your line: one army. Each chief gave up a little of his own way. That's day eight hundred fifty-nine.
